The duplication is isolated to "issue created" and "status changed" events. Those events carry multiple handlers—webhook, activity, and usage—that register together. Assignment notifications listen to different events with only a single handler, so the copy-on-write bug never affects them.

The stale unsubscribe deletes from old Set copies. The live handler map keeps the remaining handlers. Detach therefore only removes one handler per call. Re-attach then adds those same handlers again, producing duplicates.

The bug is confirmed. The `subscribe` function uses copy-on-write.

The unsubscribe callback closes over a Set snapshot captured at subscribe time. When a later subscribe copies that Set into a new Set and replaces the map entry, the earlier unsubscribe mutates the abandoned snapshot instead of the live set.

Detaching fails to remove earlier handlers. Re-attaching then adds new handlers on top of the old ones, causing duplicates.

Notifications were not duplicated because they subscribe once at module import and never re-subscribe. Later subscribers do not trigger their unsubscribe callbacks.

The fix should target the event bus unsubscribe logic directly. It must remove handlers from the live Set instead of a stale snapshot. Notification handlers should remain registered even when other event handlers are detached, since they must continue to function independently.

Re-registering without detaching first is already a no-op. Once unsubscribe correctly removes handlers from the live set, detached handlers will not produce events. After repeated detach and re-attach cycles, each action must still yield exactly one result.

The copy-on-write pattern is intentional. It prevents `emit()` from mutating the handler set while iterating over it. The bug is that unsubscribe mutates a stale snapshot instead of the live set.

The proposed fix copies the live handler set on unsubscribe and deletes the handler from that copy. A subtlety remains if this copy happens while emit() is iterating over the set.

`emit()` spreads the handler set into an array before iterating, so mutating the live Set during `emit()` does not affect the current cycle. The copy-on-write pattern on subscribe is therefore only needed to prevent a handler that attaches another handler during `emit()` from being included in that same iteration.

The fix handles multiple subscriptions and repeated unsubscriptions correctly. A handler removed by one unsubscribe cannot be removed again. The edge case of subscribing during an unsubscribe is unlikely.

A handler attaching a new subscription during emit() is handled correctly. The current emit cycle continues unaffected because it iterates over the spread array. JavaScript's single-threaded execution prevents interleaving between subscribe and unsubscribe operations. Sequential unsubscribes are also safe since each step copies the live set. The analysis then turns to a potential subtle bug in the subscribe function itself.

The copy-on-write pattern will be preserved on both subscribe and unsubscribe to maintain the documented invariant. The analysis is now turning to the `onHandlerError` function.
